answer.short: For scores $3,4,5,6,7,8$, the frequencies are $2,4,9,8,5,2$. $\Sigma f=30$.

content.prompt:
A swim club records the time each swimmer takes to swim 50 m.

Classify the type of data if:

children.label: a
children.prompt: Times are recorded in seconds, such as 31.46 s.

answer.worked: Numerical continuous — a time in seconds can take any value in a range.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Times are recorded as one of 30 s, 35 s, 40 s or 45 s.

answer.worked: Numerical discrete — the recorded response is one of four separate times, although time itself is continuous.

children.label: c
children.prompt: In part b, could a recorded time be 32 s?

answer.short: No. Only 30 s, 35 s, 40 s and 45 s can be recorded.
answer.worked: The recorded values are restricted to four separate options, so 32 s cannot be recorded. This is why the data in part b is discrete.

A bakery sells 47 pies. The table shows the number of customers who bought each number of pies. Complete the missing frequency in the table.

answer.worked:
The one-, three- and four-pie customers account for $$1\times9+3\times6+4\times2=35\text{ pies}.$$ Customers who bought no pies contribute no pies, so the remaining pies were bought by two-pie customers.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Remaining pies}&=47-35\\&=12\\\text{Two-pie customers}&=12\div2\\&=6\end{align*}$$
Check: $0\times4+1\times9+2\times6+3\times6+4\times2=47\text{ pies}$.

classification.difficultyReason: One unscaffolded missing frequency. The student must treat the 47 as a total, multiply value by frequency, subtract from 47, then divide by 2. This is simpler than p7-q12, which has two unknowns and uses the game count.

content.prompt:

The total number of kayaks was 36.

answer.short:
4 kayaks per circle

Count 9 whole-circle equivalents, including the halves, then divide 36 by 9.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Whole-circle equivalents}&=3+2\frac{1}{2}+3\frac{1}{2}\\&=9\\\text{Kayaks per circle}&=36\div9\\&=4\end{align*}$$
Each whole circle represents 4 kayaks.

classification.difficultyReason: Same structure as p9-q4. Count whole and half circles across rows (9 in total) and divide the total by that count; smaller counts make the arithmetic marginally easier.

content.prompt:
Hamish counted the pies sold at the school canteen from Monday to Thursday. The total number of pies sold was 60.

How many pies does each symbol represent?

answer.short:
5 pies per symbol

Count 12 whole-symbol equivalents, including the halves, then divide 60 by 12.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Symbols}&=3+2\tfrac{1}{2}+4\tfrac{1}{2}+2\\&=12\\12\times\text{key}&=60\\\text{key}&=60\div12\\&=5\end{align*}$$
Each symbol represents 5 pies.

content.prompt:

answer.short: Week 1. Year 9 borrowed 30 books in Week 1 and 18 in Week 5. The scales are different, so the bar lengths cannot be compared directly.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Week 1 Year 9}&=30\\\text{Week 5 Year 9}&=18\\30&>18\end{align*}$$
Year 9 borrowed more books in Week 1. The Week 5 bar is longer only because its scale is smaller.
